subject: Archaeology
title: The Archaeological Dig: How It Works
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Archaeological Dig: How It Works.

hook.text: Digging is the easy part. The hard part is recording every speck of dirt before it is gone forever.

buildup.text: Excavation is destructive — once a layer is removed, it can never be put back. Archaeologists call it 'unrepeatable.'

discovery.text: Sites are divided into square trenches using string grids. Every object is mapped in three dimensions before removal.

twist.text: Most archaeologists spend far more time writing notes, taking photos, and drawing plans than actually digging.

climax.text: Modern digs use total stations, drones, and photogrammetry — but the trowel and brush remain the core tools.

punchline.text: Digging destroys the evidence. The records are the real discovery.

quiz.question: Why is excavation considered 'unrepeatable'?
options: Government permits only allow one excavation per site
Once a layer is removed, it can never be put back — context is destroyed
Archaeological sites can only form once in geological history

details.summary: An archaeological dig follows a systematic process: survey, test pits, open-area excavation, recording, and analysis. Every layer of soil is documented, every artifact plotted in three dimensions. Excavation is destructive — once a layer is removed, it can never be re-examined.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding how digs work reveals why archaeology is slow and meticulous. Since excavation destroys what it studies, rigorous recording methods are the only way to preserve the information contained in the ground.
takeaways: Every artifact is plotted in three-dimensional space
Excavation is destructive — removed layers cannot be re-examined
Recording protocols preserve information the digging destroys

faq.question: Why do archaeologists dig so slowly and carefully?
faq.answer: Because digging destroys context. An artifact's meaning depends on its location, associated objects, and soil layer. Rushing through deposits loses this information forever. The recording — not the digging — is the actual product of an excavation.

faq.question: What happens to artifacts after they are excavated?
faq.answer: Artifacts are cleaned, cataloged, photographed, and analyzed in laboratories. Specialists study pottery, bones, metals, and organic remains. Results are published in reports. Objects are stored in repositories for future study, as new analytical techniques may extract more information later.
